3.2 — Projectiles: Instantiate, Fire, Destroy

Your turret knows when you are near; now it needs teeth. Spawning and firing a projectile looks complicated, but it breaks into four smaller problems: spawn a clone → aim it → move it → clean it up. Each of those has more than one valid solution, and today you pick yours on purpose.

Read the Docs ~15 min

Firing a projectile means coordinating four separate engine features:

Sub-problemUnity APIWhat it does
1. Spawning Instantiate(prefab, pos, rot) Creates a brand-new clone of a prefab at runtime and drops it into the scene hierarchy.
2. Aiming (target - origin).normalized Vector subtraction gives a vector pointing at the target; .normalized shrinks its length to exactly 1 so it describes direction only.
3. Moving Transform or Rigidbody2D Advances the projectile every frame. Three different ways — see the table below.
4. Cleanup Destroy(gameObject, delay) Destroys the clone after a time delay, so bullets that miss do not fly forever.

Socratic: Choosing How Your Bullet Flies

Three legitimate ways to move a projectile. Read the cost column carefully — two of these require a component the prefab does not have:

ApproachHow it worksWhat it requiresPick it when
Translate by a direction vector Keep the aim direction from spawn and offset the position by direction * speed * Time.deltaTime each frame. Nothing. Works with the prefab as it ships. Straight-flying shots that pass over or through everything.
Rotate, then move along local forward Point the sprite at the target once, then translate along its own right axis each frame. Nothing extra, but more maths. When the sprite should visibly face the way it travels — arrows, spears, missiles.
Rigidbody2D velocity Set the body's velocity once and let the physics engine carry it. A Rigidbody2D, which the projectile does not have yet. Bullets that should bounce off walls, or be stopped by them.
  1. Open Assets/Prefabs/Turret_Projectile and read its Inspector. Which of the three approaches can you build right now, and which one costs you an added component?
  2. If you want bullets that ricochet off cave walls like a pinball, which approach is dramatically easier, and what would the other two require you to build yourself?
  3. For a beam or a magic missile that flies straight through scenery, why is the direction-vector approach both simpler and more correct?
  4. Why is Destroy(gameObject, delay) essential? What happens to your frame rate if a player dodges a thousand bullets and nothing ever removes them?
  5. Your turret's range check runs every frame. If you fire from inside that check, how many bullets per second are you creating — and is that a design decision or an accident?
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Each snippet in isolation, from a system that is not a video game. Work out what maps onto your projectile.

Example 1 — Computing a heading on an aircraft navigation system:

// (destination - current) gives direction; .normalized scales the length to 1.0
Vector3 heading = (waypoint.position - transform.position).normalized;

Example 2 — Converting a direction to an angle on a weather vane:

// Atan2 turns X/Y components into an angle in radians; Rad2Deg converts to degrees
float windAngle = Mathf.Atan2(wind.y, wind.x) * Mathf.Rad2Deg;

Example 3 — Building a 2D rotation from that angle:

// In 2D, rotation happens around the Z axis - the one pointing out of the screen
transform.rotation = Quaternion.AngleAxis(windAngle, Vector3.forward);

Example 4 — Spawning and initialising on a fountain:

// Stamp a clone, then reach into it to hand over the data it needs
GameObject orb = Instantiate(orbPrefab, nozzle.position, Quaternion.identity);
orb.GetComponent<MagicOrb>().InitializeOrb(targetCoords);

Example 5 — Timed self-cleanup on a soap bubble:

// Schedules this object to be destroyed automatically 4 seconds from now
Destroy(gameObject, 4.0f);

Predict Before Building

  1. In Example 1, what happens if you leave off .normalized? If the waypoint is 20 units away and you multiply that vector by a speed, what goes wrong?
  2. Why is Vector3.forward — that is, (0, 0, 1) — the axis of rotation for a 2D sprite?
  3. In Example 4, why does the fountain reach into the clone to pass data, rather than the clone finding the target on its own? Which approach would you pick for a bullet, and why?
  4. Example 4 uses Quaternion.identity for the spawn rotation. Is that the right choice for a bullet that is about to be aimed? What does identity actually mean?
Build Lab: Your Turn ~25 min

Open Assets/Prefabs/Turret_Projectile. You will find an empty Projectile component already attached — same pattern as the turret. Your job is to fill it in.

Architectural specification for Projectile.cs:

Variables and tuning knobs:

  • What serialized float knobs should a designer be able to turn? You need at least a speed and a lifetime — are there others your chosen approach implies?
  • What defaults make sense? Think about how big the Overworld is and how far a bullet should reasonably travel before giving up.
  • Your projectile needs to remember its direction (or its target). What type holds that, and where does it get set?

Being initialised at spawn:

  • When the turret creates a bullet, it needs to tell that bullet where to go. What public method signature receives that information? Why must it be public?
  • How do you compute a direction from the spawn point to the target? Why normalize it?
  • If you chose the rotate-then-move approach: which trigonometric function gives you an angle from X and Y, and how do you convert radians to degrees?
  • If you chose the rotate-then-move approach: which axis does a 2D sprite rotate around, and which method builds a rotation from an angle and an axis?
  • How do you schedule the bullet's own destruction so it cleans up even if it never hits anything?

Flight, every frame:

  • Which method moves the transform each frame, and how do you keep the speed frame-rate independent?
  • If you rotated the sprite, which local direction is "forward" for a 2D sprite? If you did not rotate it, what do you translate by instead?
  • Why does the direction get computed once at spawn rather than recomputed every frame? What weapon would re-aiming every frame actually give you?
Architectural specification for TurretController.cs:

Inspector slots:

  • What serialized fields let a designer hand the turret a projectile to fire and a place to fire it from? (Remember the child object you noted in 3.1.)
  • What type holds a reference to a prefab — the asset, not an instance?

The firing method:

  • What guard check stops the method when a designer has left a slot empty?
  • Which method stamps a clone into the scene? What position and rotation should it start with?
  • How do you reach the Projectile component on the clone you just made, and what do you call on it?
  • Which object's position do you pass as the target — and should you pass a position, or the player's Transform?

Triggering it:

  • Where inside your existing range check does the firing method get called?
  • Which slots must be wired in the Inspector before you test?

Save, wire the slots, and press Play. Walk into range: a projectile appears at the muzzle and travels. Do not celebrate the fire rate yet — you are currently firing every single frame, because your range check runs every frame. That is exactly the problem the next lesson solves.

Bug Hunt: Projectile Faults

  1. Leave the projectile prefab slot unassigned and step into range. What error appears, and which line of your code is it pointing at?
  2. Comment out the Destroy line, fire for ten seconds, then look at the Hierarchy in play mode. How many objects are there? What will that do to the game over a five-minute session?
  3. Remove .normalized from your direction calculation. What happens when the player is far away versus close? Explain the relationship between distance and speed that you just created.
  4. Pass the player's Transform into your spawn method instead of their position, and have the bullet read targetTransform.position every frame. What kind of weapon did you accidentally build?
  5. If you chose the rotate-then-move approach, translate by Vector3.up instead of the forward direction. Which way do bullets now travel relative to where the sprite points?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Bullet tuning

  1. Tune your speed knob from something slow and dodgeable to something that feels like a sniper. At what point does the turret stop being a challenge and start being unfair? What else could you change to keep it fair at high speed?
  2. Change the lifetime knob so bullets die almost immediately, then so they live far too long. What is the right lifetime for a bullet that should threaten the player but not wander the whole map?
  3. Your bullets currently fly through everything — walls included. Is that a problem for this game? What would you have to add to a bullet to make a wall stop it, and which of the three movement approaches from the docs would then be the better choice?
  4. Fire one bullet and watch it in the Hierarchy. What is the clone named, and where does it sit in the hierarchy? Does that tell you anything about Instantiate you did not expect?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break projectile firing into spawning, aiming, moving and cleanup
  • Explain the role of Instantiate in stamping runtime clones
  • Explain why a direction vector is normalized, and what goes wrong without it
  • Compare the three ways to move a projectile, and state what each one costs
  • Explain why your turret currently fires every frame
  • Commit and push
